subs.title: SELECT basics: columns, * and expressions
subs.theory:
What it is

SELECT chooses which columns a query returns. FROM names the table. The result is a new temporary table; the stored data does not change.

Syntax

SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;
SELECT * FROM table_name;

How it works

  • * returns every column, fine for learning but avoid it in real apps (slow, fragile).
  • You can calculate: marks*1.1, or join text with ||.
  • AS renames a result column (alias).

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the comma between column names.
  • Using SELECT * on huge tables.
  • Writing the alias in quotes only when it has spaces.
subs.task: Show each student's name and marks, with marks out of 100 shown as 'percent'.
subs.starter: SELECT name, marks AS percent FROM students;

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students;
SELECT name, marks FROM students;

demo.say: A calculated column with an alias.
demo.code: SELECT name, marks+5 AS marks_with_bonus FROM students;
SELECT name || ' lives in ' || city AS info FROM students;

subs.title: DISTINCT: remove duplicates
subs.theory:
What it is

DISTINCT keeps only one copy of each repeated row in the result. It looks at the whole row of selected columns, not one column.

Syntax

SELECT DISTINCT column1 FROM table_name;
SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2 FROM table_name;

How it works

  • Without DISTINCT the city 'Noida' appears once per student.
  • With two columns, a row is a duplicate only if both values match.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts unique cities.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking DISTINCT applies only to the first column.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide a bad join instead of fixing it.
subs.task: Count how many different cities the students come from.
subs.starter: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities FROM students;

demo.code: SELECT city FROM students;
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;
SELECT DISTINCT city, marks FROM students;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM students;

subs.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT
subs.theory:
What it is

ORDER BY sorts the result. ASC (smallest first) is the default, DESC is largest first. LIMIT returns only the first n rows, so ORDER BY + LIMIT gives 'top n'.

Syntax

SELECT cols FROM t ORDER BY col1 DESC, col2 ASC LIMIT 3;

How it works

  • Sorting by several columns: ties in the first are broken by the next.
  • Text sorts alphabetically, numbers numerically.
  • ORDER BY runs near the end, so it can use column aliases.

Common mistakes

  • Using LIMIT without ORDER BY and expecting the 'best' rows.
  • Forgetting DESC when asked for highest first.
subs.task: Show the top 3 students by marks.
subs.starter: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

demo.code: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks;
SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;
SELECT city, name, marks FROM students ORDER BY city ASC, marks DESC;
SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

topics.title: WHERE, AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN

subs.title: WHERE and comparison operators
subs.theory:
What it is

WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true. It runs before grouping and sorting.

Syntax

SELECT cols FROM t WHERE column operator value;

How it works

  • Operators: = <> > < >= <=.
  • Text values go in single quotes, numbers do not.
  • Use <> (or !=) for 'not equal'.

Common mistakes

  • Using == instead of =.
  • Writing text without quotes.
  • Putting aggregate functions in WHERE (use HAVING).
subs.task: Find students with marks of 75 or more.
subs.starter: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks>=75;

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Delhi';
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks>70;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city<>'Noida';

subs.title: AND, OR, NOT
subs.theory:
What it is

AND needs both conditions true, OR needs at least one, NOT reverses a condition. AND is evaluated before OR, so use brackets to be clear.

Syntax

WHERE cond1 AND cond2
WHERE cond1 OR cond2
WHERE NOT cond

How it works

  • Brackets decide order: A AND (B OR C).
  • NOT works with other operators: NOT IN, NOT LIKE, IS NOT NULL.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing AND and OR without brackets and getting unexpected rows.
subs.task: Find Noida students with marks above 60, or any student with marks above 90.
subs.starter: SELECT * FROM students WHERE (city='Noida' AND marks>60) OR marks>90;

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida' AND marks>70;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Delhi' OR marks<60;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE NOT city='Noida';
SELECT * FROM students WHERE (city='Noida' AND marks>60) OR marks>90;

subs.title: LIKE and wildcards
subs.theory:
What it is

LIKE searches text by pattern. % means any number of characters, _ means exactly one character.

Syntax

WHERE column LIKE 'pattern'

How it works

  • 'A%' starts with A; '%a' ends with a; '%an%' contains an.
  • '_i%' second letter is i.
  • Case rules depend on the database (PostgreSQL has ILIKE for case-insensitive).

Common mistakes

  • Using = with wildcards (= does not understand %).
  • Forgetting the quotes around the pattern.
subs.task: Find students whose name has exactly 4 letters.
subs.starter: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name LIKE '____';

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';
SELECT * FROM students WHERE name LIKE '%an%';
SELECT * FROM students WHERE name LIKE '_i%';

subs.title: IN and BETWEEN
subs.theory:
What it is

IN checks if a value is in a list (a short form of many ORs). BETWEEN checks an inclusive range (both ends included).

Syntax

WHERE col IN (v1, v2)
WHERE col BETWEEN low AND high

How it works

  • BETWEEN 60 AND 80 includes 60 and 80.
  • NOT IN and NOT BETWEEN reverse them.
  • IN also accepts a subquery.

Common mistakes

  • Writing BETWEEN 80 AND 60 (low value must come first).
  • Using NOT IN with a list that contains NULL (returns nothing).
subs.task: Find students from Delhi or Lucknow with marks between 70 and 95.
subs.starter: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city IN ('Delhi','Lucknow') AND marks BETWEEN 70 AND 95;

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city IN ('Delhi','Lucknow');
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 80;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 80;

subs.title: NULL values
subs.theory:
What it is

NULL means 'unknown or missing', not zero and not empty text. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, so normal operators fail.

Syntax

WHERE col IS NULL
WHERE col IS NOT NULL
COALESCE(col, default)

How it works

  • col = NULL never matches; use IS NULL.
  • COUNT(col) ignores NULLs, COUNT(*) does not.
  • COALESCE replaces NULL with a default.

Common mistakes

  • Writing = NULL.
  • Forgetting that NULL affects averages and totals.
subs.task: Insert a student with no city and find them.
subs.starter:
INSERT INTO students(name,marks) VALUES('Zoya',88);
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

demo.code: INSERT INTO students(name,marks) VALUES('Zoya',88);
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = NULL;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

demo.say: Show a default instead of NULL.
demo.code: SELECT name, COALESCE(city,'Unknown') AS city FROM students;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE changes rows, DELETE ... WHERE removes rows. Forgetting WHERE affects every row. NULL means unknown: test with IS NULL, never = NULL.

subs.starter:

UPDATE students SET city='Noida' WHERE name='Zoya';

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: MIN, MAX, COUNT, SUM, AVG summarise many rows into one value. AS gives a column or table a temporary name. COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs.

topics.title: JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, SELF, CROSS)

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: A join combines rows of two tables using a condition. INNER: only matches. LEFT: all left rows + matches. RIGHT: all right rows. FULL: everything. SELF: a table joined with itself. CROSS: every combination.
subs.task: List every student with their course name, including students with no course.

demo.say: INNER JOIN: only students who enrolled.
demo.code: SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid JOIN courses c ON c.cid=e.cid;

demo.say: LEFT JOIN keeps students with no course (NULL).
demo.code: SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.cid=e.cid;

demo.code: SELECT a.name, b.name, a.city FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.city=b.city AND a.id<b.id;
SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c LIMIT 6;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: UNION merges results and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them. GROUP BY makes groups for aggregates. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
subs.task: Cities where the average marks are above 70.
subs.starter: SELECT city, AVG(marks) FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING AVG(marks)>70;

demo.code: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;

SELECT city FROM students UNION SELECT cname FROM courses;
SELECT city FROM students UNION ALL SELECT city FROM students;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: A subquery is a query inside a query. IN checks a list; EXISTS checks that rows exist (stops at first match). Correlated subqueries refer to the outer row. CASE adds if/else logic. ANY/ALL are not in SQLite: practise them in the PostgreSQL tab.

subs.theory: DDL defines structure. Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT, AUTO INCREMENT (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite, SERIAL in PostgreSQL).

subs.theory: A view is a saved query. An index speeds up searches on a column. SQL injection: attacker input changes the query, e.g. ' OR '1'='1. Defence: parameterised / prepared statements, never string concatenation.
subs.task: Create a view of students scoring above 80.

dbms.title: DBMS
dbms.seed: CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT,city TEXT,marks INTEGER);INSERT INTO students VALUES(1,'Aman','Noida',82),(2,'Riya','Delhi',91);

subs.title: File system vs DBMS
subs.theory:
What it is

A file system stores data in separate files managed by each application. A DBMS keeps data in one organised system with shared rules, so many users and programs can use it safely.

Syntax

Flat file: one file per application  vs  DBMS: one database, many applications

How it works

  • Redundancy: same data stored many times.
  • Inconsistency: copies disagree after an update.
  • Concurrency problems: two users update together and one change is lost.
  • Isolation and security: hard to control who sees what.

Common mistakes

  • Believing a spreadsheet is a DBMS.
  • Thinking redundancy is always zero in a DBMS (it is controlled, not removed).
subs.task: Create a flat table and show how an update makes data inconsistent.

demo.say: Student data is repeated on every row (redundancy). If you see 'already exists', press Reset database.
Update only one row: Aman now has two cities (inconsistency).
demo.code:
UPDATE flat SET city='Delhi' WHERE course='SQL';
SELECT * FROM flat;

subs.title: Three-schema architecture
subs.theory:
What it is

The database is described at three levels so that users, designers and storage can change independently.

Syntax

External level (views)  <-  Conceptual level (tables)  <-  Internal level (files, indexes)

How it works

  • External: what each user sees (views).
  • Conceptual: the logical design of the whole database (tables, keys).
  • Internal: how data is physically stored (files, indexes, blocks).
  • Mappings connect the levels.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up conceptual and internal levels.
  • Thinking a view stores its own data (it stores only a query).
subs.task: Create a view that shows only names and cities (hiding marks).
subs.starter:
CREATE VIEW public_info AS SELECT name, city FROM students;
SELECT * FROM public_info;

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students;

demo.say: External level: a view for a limited user.
demo.code:
CREATE VIEW public_info AS SELECT name, city FROM students;
SELECT * FROM public_info;

demo.say: Internal level: the catalog stores the structure.
demo.code: SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master;

subs.title: Data independence
subs.theory:
What it is

Data independence means one level can change without breaking the level above it.

Syntax

Physical independence: change storage, logical schema stays.
Logical independence: change schema, user views/apps stay.

How it works

  • Physical: adding an index changes how data is stored; queries are unchanged.
  • Logical: adding a column should not break existing views and programs.
  • Logical independence is harder to achieve.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking an index changes the query text.
  • Expecting all schema changes to be harmless.
subs.task: Add an index and a new column, then re-run an old query.

demo.code: CREATE INDEX idx_city ON students(city);

demo.say: The old query still works unchanged.
demo.code: SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

demo.say: Logical change: add a column. The view from the previous subtopic keeps working.
demo.code:
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;
SELECT name, city FROM students;

subs.title: DBMS components
subs.theory:
What it is

A DBMS is built from cooperating parts. Understanding them explains what happens when a query runs.

Syntax

Query -> DDL/DML compiler -> optimizer -> execution engine -> storage manager

How it works

  • DDL compiler processes CREATE/ALTER; DML compiler processes SELECT/INSERT.
  • Query optimizer picks the cheapest plan.
  • Execution engine runs the plan.
  • Storage and buffer manager read and cache disk blocks.
  • Transaction and lock managers keep ACID and control concurrency.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the optimizer changes the answer (it only changes the speed).
subs.task: View the plan the optimizer chose for a query.
subs.starter: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks>70;

demo.say: The data dictionary (catalog) is stored by the DBMS itself.
demo.code: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master;
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks>70;

subs.title: Data models
subs.theory:
What it is

A data model is the way data and relationships are organised.

Syntax

Hierarchical (tree), Network (graph), Relational (tables), Object-oriented (objects)

How it works

  • Hierarchical: parent-child tree, one parent per child.
  • Network: records linked in a graph, many parents allowed.
  • Relational: tables (rows and columns) joined by keys; the most common model.
  • Object-oriented: data and behaviour stored as objects.

Common mistakes

  • Calling a document database relational (see the MongoDB tab).
subs.task: Show a relationship in the relational model using a join.
subs.starter: SELECT s.name, e.cid FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid;

demo.say: Tables are linked by key values.
demo.code: SELECT * FROM enrol;
SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid JOIN courses c ON c.cid=e.cid;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• Entities, strong vs weak, attributes: simple, composite, multi-valued, derived.
  • Cardinality 1:1, 1:N, M:N. Participation total vs partial. Degree: unary, binary, ternary.
  • EER: specialization, generalization, inheritance, aggregation, categorization.
  • Mapping rules: entity = table; M:N = junction table; multi-valued attribute = own table; weak entity = table with owner's key in its primary key.
subs.task: Map a weak entity 'Dependent' of 'Employee' to tables.
subs.starter:
CREATE TABLE employee(eid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ename TEXT);
CREATE TABLE dependent(eid INTEGER, dname TEXT, PRIMARY KEY(eid,dname), FOREIGN KEY(eid) REFERENCES employee(eid) ON DELETE CASCADE);

demo.code: CREATE TABLE employee(eid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ename TEXT);

demo.say: Weak entity: key = owner key + partial key.
demo.code: CREATE TABLE dependent(eid INTEGER, dname TEXT, PRIMARY KEY(eid,dname), FOREIGN KEY(eid) REFERENCES employee(eid) ON DELETE CASCADE);

demo.say: Multi-valued attribute (phones) gets its own table.
demo.code: CREATE TABLE emp_phone(eid INTEGER, phone TEXT, PRIMARY KEY(eid,phone));

demo.say: M:N relationship becomes a junction table (see 'enrol').
demo.code: SELECT * FROM enrol;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• Constraints: domain, entity integrity (PK not null), referential integrity (FK, ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL).
  • Algebra: selection σ, projection π, product ×, union ∪, intersection ∩, difference −, joins ⋈, division ÷, rename ρ.
  • Calculus: TRC and DRC are non-procedural; safe expressions equal algebra in power.
subs.task: Write σ city='Noida' (students) and π name in SQL.
subs.starter: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

demo.say: π projection = column list (DISTINCT, because algebra returns sets).
demo.code: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;
SELECT s.name, e.cid FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid;
SELECT id FROM students EXCEPT SELECT sid FROM enrol;
SELECT id FROM students INTERSECT SELECT sid FROM enrol;

demo.say: ÷ division: students enrolled in ALL courses (needs double NOT EXISTS).
demo.code: SELECT name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT cid FROM courses c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrol e WHERE e.sid=s.id AND e.cid=c.cid));

topics.title: Module 4: SQL (DDL, DML, subqueries, views, triggers)

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• DDL/DCL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, GRANT, REVOKE.
  • DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT. Execution order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
  • Subqueries: independent vs correlated (EXISTS, IN, ALL, ANY).
  • Views: updatable vs read-only, materialised. Triggers: row-level vs statement-level. Stored procedures/functions.
subs.task: Create a trigger that logs every new student.

demo.say: Create a log table and a row-level trigger.
demo.code:
CREATE TABLE log(msg TEXT);
CREATE TRIGGER t_new AFTER INSERT ON students BEGIN INSERT INTO log VALUES('added '||NEW.name); END;
INSERT INTO students VALUES(9,'Neha','Delhi',70);
SELECT * FROM log;

demo.say: Correlated subquery: students above their own city's average.
demo.code: SELECT name, city, marks FROM students s WHERE marks>(SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students WHERE city=s.city);

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• FD X→Y. Closure X⁺, canonical cover, Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity).
  • Anomalies: insertion, deletion, modification.
  • 1NF atomic values. 2NF no partial dependency. 3NF X→A needs X superkey or A prime. BCNF X must be a superkey.
  • 4NF (MVDs), 5NF (join dependencies). Check decomposition: lossless join and dependency preservation.
subs.task: Decompose enrol_flat(sid, sname, cid, cname) into 3 tables and rebuild it by joining.

demo.say: Unnormalized table: sname depends only on sid (partial dependency).
Modification anomaly: change one row, data becomes inconsistent.
demo.code:
UPDATE enrol_flat SET sname='Aman K' WHERE sid=1 AND cid=1;
SELECT * FROM enrol_flat;

demo.say: Lossless join: joining back gives the original rows.
demo.code: SELECT e2.sid, s2.sname, e2.cid, c2.cname FROM e2 JOIN s2 ON e2.sid=s2.sid JOIN c2 ON e2.cid=c2.cid;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• Blocks, blocking factor = floor(block size / record size), fixed vs variable records, spanned vs unspanned.
  • Heap, sequential and clustered files.
  • Primary, clustering and secondary indexes; multi-level indexes.
  • B-tree vs B+ tree (all pointers in linked leaves = fast range scans).
  • Static hashing, overflow, collisions; dynamic: extendible and linear hashing.
subs.task: Create an index and compare the query plan before and after.
subs.starter: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

demo.say: Without an index: full table scan.
demo.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

demo.say: Create an index (SQLite uses a B-tree).
demo.code: CREATE INDEX idx_city ON students(city);

demo.say: Same query now uses the index.
demo.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. States: active, partially committed, committed, failed, aborted.
  • Schedules: serial, conflict/view serializability (precedence graph).
  • Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update.
  • Locking: shared S, exclusive X; 2PL (basic, conservative, strict, rigorous). Timestamp ordering, Thomas write rule, optimistic control.
  • Deadlock: wait-die, wound-wait, wait-for graph, victim selection.
subs.task: Move marks between two students inside one transaction and roll it back.

demo.code: BEGIN;

demo.say: Two updates that must succeed together.
demo.code:
UPDATE students SET marks=marks-10 WHERE id=1;
UPDATE students SET marks=marks+10 WHERE id=2;

demo.say: Inside the transaction the change is visible.
demo.code: SELECT id,marks FROM students WHERE id IN (1,2);
ROLLBACK;
SELECT id,marks FROM students WHERE id IN (1,2);

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• Failures: system crash, media failure, transaction error.
  • WAL: log before data. Log records, undo and redo.
  • Deferred update (no-undo/redo), immediate update (undo/redo), checkpoints, ARIES (analysis, redo, undo).
  • Pipeline: parse, verify, optimize, generate code.
  • Heuristic: push selections and projections down. Cost-based: size estimates, histograms, access-path costs.
subs.task: View the plan of a join query.
subs.starter: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid JOIN courses c ON c.cid=e.cid WHERE s.city='Noida';

demo.say: The optimizer chooses join order and access paths.
demo.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s JOIN enrol e ON s.id=e.sid JOIN courses c ON c.cid=e.cid WHERE s.city='Noida';

demo.say: Add an index and watch the plan change.
demo.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_enrol_sid ON enrol(sid);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM enrol WHERE sid=1;

topics.title: Module 9: Distributed, NoSQL and data warehousing

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory:
• Homogeneous vs heterogeneous; fragmentation (horizontal, vertical, hybrid); replication; 2PC.
  • CAP theorem and BASE; document, key-value, wide-column, graph stores (try the MongoDB tab).
  • OLTP vs OLAP; star, snowflake and fact-constellation schemas; ETL.

demo.code: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city='Noida';

subs.title: Data types and CREATE TABLE
subs.theory:
What it is

CREATE TABLE defines the structure: columns, data types and rules. Choosing the right type saves space and prevents bad data.

Syntax

CREATE TABLE name (
  col type constraint, ...
);

How it works

  • INT, BIGINT: whole numbers. SERIAL: auto-increasing id.
  • TEXT / VARCHAR(n): text. NUMERIC(p,s): exact decimals.
  • BOOLEAN, DATE, TIMESTAMP, JSONB.
  • Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK.

Common mistakes

  • Using FLOAT for money (use NUMERIC).
  • Forgetting PRIMARY KEY.

demo.code: CREATE TABLE books(id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, price NUMERIC(8,2) CHECK(price>0), published DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE);

subs.title: INSERT and RETURNING
subs.theory:
What it is

INSERT adds rows. PostgreSQL's RETURNING shows the stored row immediately, including generated values like SERIAL ids.

Syntax

INSERT INTO t(col1,col2) VALUES (v1,v2), (v3,v4) RETURNING *;

How it works

  • List columns explicitly so the order does not matter.
  • Several rows can be inserted in one statement.
  • Skipped columns get their DEFAULT or NULL.

Common mistakes

  • Inserting text without quotes.
  • Breaking a constraint (the whole statement fails).

subs.title: Fetching data: ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET
subs.theory:
What it is

SELECT reads data. ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT restricts the number of rows and OFFSET skips rows, which is how pagination works.

Syntax

SELECT cols FROM t ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10;

How it works

  • Page n of size k: LIMIT k OFFSET (n-1)*k.
  • Always use ORDER BY with LIMIT so results are predictable.
  • DISTINCT ON(col) keeps the first row per value (PostgreSQL feature).

Common mistakes

  • Using OFFSET on very large tables (it gets slow).

topics.title: Aggregates: MIN, MAX, COUNT, SUM, AVG

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: Aggregates collapse rows. Use FILTER (WHERE ...) for conditional aggregates and ROUND() for neat output.

topics.title: Joins: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: Same join family as SQL. PostgreSQL supports FULL JOIN natively. Use table aliases. USING(col) is a short form when both tables have the same column name.

subs.starter: SELECT c.cname, COUNT(e.sid) FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrol e ON c.cid=e.cid GROUP BY c.cname;

demo.say: FULL JOIN: unmatched rows from both sides.

SELECT s.name, c.cname FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c LIMIT 5;

topics.title: UNION, GROUP BY, HAVING, EXISTS, ANY, ALL, CASE

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: UNION merges results. HAVING filters groups. ANY: true if any value matches; ALL: true if all match. EXISTS checks for rows. CASE is if/else inside SQL.
subs.task: Find students whose marks are higher than ALL Noida students.
subs.starter: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > ALL (SELECT marks FROM students WHERE city='Noida');

demo.say: ANY: higher than at least one Noida student.
demo.code: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > ANY (SELECT marks FROM students WHERE city='Noida');

demo.say: ALL: higher than every Noida student.
demo.code: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > ALL (SELECT marks FROM students WHERE city='Noida');
SELECT name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrol e WHERE e.sid=s.id);
SELECT name, CASE WHEN marks>=90 THEN 'A' WHEN marks>=70 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END AS grade FROM students;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*)>1;

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: Window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing them: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC), ROW_NUMBER(), SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY city).

subs.title: find() and filters
subs.theory:
What it is

find() returns documents that match a filter object. An empty filter {} matches everything. Several fields in one filter mean AND.

Syntax

db.collection.find(filter)

How it works

  • Filter by equality: {city:'Noida'}.
  • Several conditions: {city:'Noida', marks:{$gt:70}}.
  • Find inside arrays: {skills:'sql'}.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting quotes around text values.
  • Expecting SQL-style case-insensitive matching (MongoDB is case sensitive).
subs.task: Find students in Noida with marks above 70.
subs.starter: db.students.find({city:'Noida', marks:{$gt:70}})

demo.code: db.students.find()

subs.title: Projection: choose fields
subs.theory:
What it is

The second argument of find() lists which fields to return. 1 includes a field, 0 hides it. _id is returned unless hidden.

Syntax

db.collection.find(filter, {field:1, _id:0})

How it works

  • Use all 1s to include, or all 0s to exclude. Do not mix (except _id).
  • Smaller results are faster and cleaner.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing 1 and 0 for normal fields.

demo.code: db.students.find({}, {name:1, marks:1})

subs.title: sort(), limit() and counting
subs.theory:
What it is

sort() orders results (1 ascending, -1 descending). limit() caps the number returned. countDocuments() counts matches.

Syntax

db.collection.find().sort({field:-1}).limit(n)
db.collection.countDocuments(filter)

How it works

  • Sort and limit together give 'top n'.
  • countDocuments({}) counts all documents.

Common mistakes

  • Writing sort({marks:'desc'}); use -1.
subs.task: Show the top 2 students by marks.
subs.starter: db.students.find({}, {name:1, marks:1, _id:0}).sort({marks:-1}).limit(2)

subs.title: Overview
subs.theory: A pipeline passes documents through stages: $match (filter), $group (group with $sum, $avg, $max, $min), $sort, $limit. This is MongoDB's GROUP BY.
subs.task: Average marks per city, highest first.
subs.starter: db.students.aggregate([{$group:{_id:'$city', avg:{$avg:'$marks'}, total:{$sum:1}}},{$sort:{avg:-1}}])

demo.code: db.students.aggregate([{$group:{_id:'$city', total:{$sum:1}}}])
db.students.aggregate([{$group:{_id:'$city', avg:{$avg:'$marks'}}},{$sort:{avg:-1}}])
db.students.aggregate([{$match:{marks:{$gt:60}}},{$group:{_id:'$city', best:{$max:'$marks'}}}])
